parties:
Golam Mohammad ----- Appellant.
Vs.
Sree Sailendra Nath Kanangoe being dead his heirs Sree Biman Behari Kanangoe and others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J. : This appeal by leave by the pre-emptee-appellant is from the judgment and order of a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division (at Chittagong) dated 25.11.85 passed in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 203 of 1978 allowing the appeal and thereby setting aside the judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong dated 25.5.78 in Miscellaneous Case No. 274 of 1976 dismissing the pre-emptor-respondents' application for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, seeking to pre-empt the transfer made by respondent Nos. 2 and 3 to the appellant by kabala dated 4.10.74 which was registered on 9.6.76. The pre-emptor-respondents earlier brought Miscellaneous Case No. 281 of 1974 for the same purpose but it was dismissed, inter alia, on the ground of maintainability by order dated 30.6.76. 

 2. The grounds on which the appellant resisted the present pre-emption case were, inter alia, that the application was barred by res judicata and that it was bad for defect of parties. The trial Court found that the case was bad for defect of party as one Amalendu Dev, a co-sharer in the disputed plot (No. 1061) was not made a party thereto. As the trial Court in the earlier Miscellaneous Case No. 281 of 1974 while discussing issue No. 4, namely, whether the case is barred under equity and justice, found that the pre-emptor-respondents did not come to the Court with clean hands, the trial Court in the present case held that its finding could operate as res judicata, the earlier decision being not only on maintainability but also on merit. The High Court Division held that the other findings in the earlier pre-emption case cannot operate as res judicata as the case was dismissed on a preliminary point of maintainability. As for defect of party the learned Judge of the High Court Division followed a decision of the High Court Division in the case of Hosne Ara Begum & ors. Vs. Mosammat Anowara Begum & others, 37 DLR 154 and held that in a proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act anyone else other than the transferees need not be impleaded as a party. The appeal was allowed on that view. 

 5. On the second point Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel for the appellant, has taken us through sections 23 and 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act which were not placed before this Court while disposing of CP No. 10 of 1974. Section 23 provides that in case of transfer of pre-emptible non-agricultural land the pre-emptor has to file notices together with process fees for service thereof on all co-sharer tenants who are not parties to the transfer. Section 24 provides that within 4 months of the service of notice or within 4 months from the date of knowledge of such transfer, if no notice has been issued or served, a co-sharer may apply to the Court for pre-emption. From all these provisions in sections 23 and 24 of the Act Mr. Ahmed submits that although no specific provision has been made requiring a pre-emptor to make all co-sharers as parties, as has been done by section 96(2) in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, it is imperative that the co-sharer-tenants must be made parties to an application under section 24 of the Act to give meaning and validity to the provision of service of notice of transfer to them and to the provision of their choice of pre-emption. Failure to add one of the co-sharers as a party will result in the failure of the application on the ground of defect of party, he submits. He further submits that the express provision of adding all co-sharer-tenants in an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was necessary because priorities have to be fixed in respect of pre-emption between co-sharers of various types and contiguous owners, but in respect of pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act only the co-sharers can apply for pre-emption and there is no provision for fixation of priority among them. As such no specific provision was made in the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act requiring co-sharers to be added as parties. He also submits that in the absence of any provision as to who may be added as parties in a proceeding under section 24, the procedural law, namely, Order I, rule 3 and Order I rule 10(2) CPC will govern the field. 

 7. It is clear that the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act does not in terms require a pre-emptor to mandatorily make all co-sharers as parties to the proceeding under section 24 in the same way as section 96(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act does in respect of a proceeding under that section. Nor can such mandatory requirement be inferred from the language of sections 23(4) and 24 (4) of the said Act. In the absence of any specific provision in the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act as to who are to be made parties in an application under section 24, the procedural law, namely, Order 1, rule 3 or Order 1 rule 10(2) CPC will govern the field. Hence in each case the pre-emptee has to make out a case as to whether a left-out co-sharer was a necessary or proper party. In a proceeding under section 24 the transferee is a necessary party as the pre-emptor seeks relief against him and as the purchase of the transferee is under challenge, but the pre-emptor seeks no relief against any co-sharer. The co-sharers are, therefore, not necessary parties in terms of Order 1 rule 3 CPC. Nor are they proper parties unless the co-sharers themselves pray to the Court to add them as parties on the ground of non-receipt of notice or lack of knowledge or any other acceptable ground. In a proceeding under section 24 of the Act it will be presumed that all co-sharers have received the requisite notices under section 23(1) of the Act unless any so-sharer prefers to rebut that presumption. Hence we do not find any cogent reason to re-consider the decision of this Court in the case of Shafique Mia Vs. Meherunnessa and another, CP No. 10 of 1974.
